title: Only Answer in This Shape

post.author: u/register_room_ysbrand
post.title: I built the program that fills in our county's death register overnight. Every form comes out perfect. Last night it wrote down when and how a man died. Nobody has examined him yet.

blocks.text: I'm the night clerk at the Saltmere County coroner's office, and a junior developer, which is why the night clerk has a program now. Officers, doctors and care homes leave a handwritten note for every death they report. I type each note in exactly as it's written, and my program fills in the death register's form from it.

It sends the note to a language model and asks for the form back as JSON, plain text made of named fields and values, which code can read. Until last month I asked for it in the prompt, with one filled-in example, and parsed whatever came back, which means reading the text into those fields. About one reply in four wouldn't parse: a polite sentence where the form should be, or JSON with its end missing. Those notes waited for me.

Three weeks ago I switched on the provider's structured outputs, a setting that makes every reply fit a schema you send with the request. A schema is a description of a form, written in JSON. Mine is the register's form.

blocks.title: THE FORM, as my schema has it

blocks.text: Since then, not one failure. Last night there were sixteen notes, and the program made sixteen forms, every box filled. This was the fourteenth.

05:52  note, as typed
       05:10. Bus shelter, Sallow Road. Found, unidentified.
05:52  form
       {"name": "unidentified", "age": 64, "found_at": "05:10",
        "place": "Bus shelter, Sallow Road",
        "time_of_death": "02:40", "cause": "exposure"}
He has no name yet. The register already knows when he died, and how.

At eight Dr Ottilie Marsk, the deputy coroner, read the night's entries and came down to the register room. Nobody has examined him, she said. Nobody knows when he died, or how. Then she asked me who had told the register.
She has switched the program off until I can explain it. What happened, and what do I change?

blocks.label: form_14.png

diagram.aria: Ysbrand's drawing of how the fourteenth form was made. Top row: the note, the man found at 05:10 in the Sallow Road bus shelter, which says only found, unidentified, is typed in and goes to the model, which has structured outputs on and fits every reply to the schema; the schema, six boxes, all required, with three choices for cause, goes to the model as the form. Bottom row: the model fills the record, age 64, died 02:40, cause exposure, which is written to the register as entry 14 of 16, though he has not yet been examined; and the same happened for every note last night: 16 notes, 16 forms, every box filled.

notes.text: how the fourteenth form was made

blocks.caption: Drawn at nine this morning. At 05:52 I typed in the patrol's note, which says where he was found and when, and nothing else. The model filled in the form against my schema: six boxes, all required, and a cause that has to be natural, accident or exposure. All sixteen of last night's forms came back like this one, every box filled.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in the register room is haunted. The model behind your program read one note and filled one form, the way it filled the other fifteen. A few names for what you built. Your schema is a JSON Schema: a JSON document that sets the rules another one must follow, such as which fields it has and what type of value each holds. A required field must be present in every form. An enum is a fixed list of the only values a field may hold; your cause box is one. And structured outputs work by constrained decoding: as the model picks each next token, as in case 6, the provider gives no chance at all to any token that would break your schema. Two questions. On a night when a note doesn't say how someone died, which values can your cause box hold? And put each of last night's sixteen forms beside its note: which values can you find written in the note?

replies.author: u/register_room_ysbrand
replies.text: Natural, accident or exposure. Nothing else. I put all sixteen forms beside their notes. Eleven have every value written in their notes, though one of those says Ernest Vellacott is 1958 years old, the year he was born, and my schema says 120 at most. Five don't: eight values that no note holds, three of them his. All five notes said, one way or another, that nobody knew: last seen Sunday, age not known, time of death not known, cause for the coroner, and found, unidentified. Then I ran last night's notes through my old prompt-only program. Four replies it couldn't read, seven forms with a box wrong, and for the man at Sallow Road it left out his age, his time and his cause. My program called that broken. It was the truth.

comments.author: u/old_register_hephzibah
comments.text: I kept the Saltmere register by hand from 1979 until the computers came. The printed form had no box for not known either, and the county wanted every box filled before the book went off at the end of each month. So when a cause wasn't known yet, we wrote in the likeliest one, in pencil, to be rubbed out when the pathologist's report came. Most were rubbed out and inked over with the right one. Hold the old books up to a lamp and you can still see the pencil under the ink.

replies.author: u/register_room_ysbrand
replies.text: Dr Marsk says she still finds them.

comments.author: u/payables_wendeline
comments.text: Same thing at work, without the lamp. Our invoice reader turns supplier invoices into records for the payments system, and its schema requires a purchase order number, eight digits. Invoices without one got one anyway: eight digits that looked exactly right. Our validator, the code that checks each record against the schema before it goes on, passed every one, because every one had the right shape. Finance paid two of them before anyone asked what had been ordered.

reply.prompt: Dr Marsk will switch the program back on tonight if Ysbrand can show it won't happen again. What should he change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Switch structured outputs off and go back to the prompt with its example. The old program stopped on replies it couldn't read and left boxes out when a note didn't say, so it never made anything up.
options.verdict: Breakage instead of invention, and still one invention
options.part2: Structured outputs went off at noon, and the prompt and its example came back. Before the night began I ran last night's sixteen notes through it. Four replies wouldn't parse, and those notes waited for me. Twelve forms went on to the register, and seven had a box it couldn't use: an age of about 70, a cause of road collision, a time of 5.40am, a time of death of not known, and three with boxes left out, the man at Sallow Road's among them. And Isadora Fitch's note says cause for the coroner. Her form says natural.
options.senior: Asking in the prompt is the weakest of the three ways to get structure: replies come back as prose, broken JSON or the wrong types, and the model still guesses where it can. Going back trades a quiet invention for noisy breakage, and nothing checks either.

options.text: Keep structured outputs and give the form an honest box: the cause may be unknown, and age and time of death may be left empty. Then the model always has somewhere to put what a note doesn't say.
options.verdict: Trade-off: an honest box, and nobody checking
options.part2: The cause box got unknown, and age and time of death may now be empty. I ran the sixteen again: sixteen forms. The man at Sallow Road is unidentified, with no age, no time and cause unknown, and three other notes that didn't say got empty boxes too. Fourteen forms match their notes. Two don't. Isadora Fitch's still says natural, because her note says she looked peaceful. And Ernest Vellacott is still 1958 years old: nothing checks a form before it reaches the register.
options.senior: An explicit unknown is the biggest single fix: a required box with no honest answer invites a guess, and under structured outputs forces one. But a schema shapes what the model may write, not whether it's true, and the provider doesn't enforce every rule in it. Your own code still has to check each form before it's written.

options.text: Keep the schema as it is, and add one line to the prompt: if the note doesn't say, don't guess. Structured outputs keep every form complete, and the line keeps the model from making up what goes in it.
options.part2: The line went in at noon, and I ran last night's sixteen again. Sixteen forms, every box filled. The same five forms held values no note had given: eight values, and the man at Sallow Road still 64 years old, dead at 02:40, of exposure. The cause box still offered three answers, and don't know wasn't one of them. Ernest Vellacott was still 1958.
options.senior: With structured outputs on, the provider only lets the model write what the schema allows. An instruction to admit it doesn't know can't be followed when the schema has no way to say so. Change the form, not just the words around it, and check what comes back.

options.text: Give the form honest boxes for not known, and keep structured outputs. Then check every form in code: the whole schema, then each value against its note. Ask again once with the error; anything still wrong goes to Dr Marsk.
options.part2: Unknown went into the cause box, and age and time of death may now be empty. The program checks every form in code: first the whole schema, the age range included, then that every value is written in its note. A form that fails gets one more try, with the error added; if it fails again it goes to Dr Marsk's queue. On the sixteen there were two second tries. Ernest Vellacott's age came back as 67. Isadora Fitch's cause came back as natural again, and went to the queue, and Dr Marsk read the note herself and marked it pending. Fifteen forms reached the register, every value in them written in a note. The man at Sallow Road is unidentified, with no age, no time, and cause unknown. On Thursday his sister came in and gave him his name back. The cause still says unknown, because nobody knows it yet.
options.senior: Let the provider enforce the shape, and design the shape so not known is a legal answer. Then check in your own code anyway: the rules the provider skips, and what each value means. Ask again once with the error, then hand it to a person. Nothing unchecked reaches the record.

sim.title: Run the coroner's form lab yourself
sim.lede: You're Ysbrand at nine in the morning with last night's sixteen notes. The replies here are recorded teaching outputs, written for this case: a teaching simplification of the kinds of replies models give, such as sentences, broken JSON, the wrong types, boxes left out, values made up to fill a box and honest blanks. They are not a measurement of any model or provider. Each note has a first reply for each way of asking, with unknown allowed or not, and a second reply for when the program asks again. The validator, a few lines of plain code, checks a parsed reply against the schema: every box present, each the right type, the cause from the list, the age from 0 to 120, times like 05:10, and null, JSON's word for no value, only where unknown is allowed. The semantic check, a check of what a value means rather than its shape, asks one thing: is every value written in the note? Pick a strategy. 1, prompt only, parses what comes back and passes it on to the register. 2, schema-constrained, uses structured outputs and passes the reply on. 3 validates every reply and, on a failure, asks once more with the error added, then returns an error. 4 does the same, then sends what is still wrong to a person. Strategies 3 and 4 can ask either way, and only they use the semantic check. The grid and the table show every strategy's counts at once: parsed, valid, invented but valid, second tries, sent to a person, errors, and passed on.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you start where Ysbrand did, on strategy 2 with no unknown and note 14 shown: the man at Sallow Road gets age 64, time of death 02:40 and cause exposure. All 16 replies parse and are passed on; 5 forms hold invented values, 8 in all, and note 7 says Ernest Vellacott is 1958. Pick strategy 1: 4 replies won't parse, 8 of the 12 passed on are wrong, and note 14 comes back with three boxes left out. Pick strategy 3 and set it to ask with the prompt: 11 second tries and 1 error, note 13, still a sentence, but 5 invented forms are passed on, and 4 of them were honest gaps that the second try filled in. Turn the semantic check on: 12 second tries, 6 errors and 10 forms passed on, none wrong. Allow unknown: 8 second tries, 2 errors, 14 passed on. Now set it to ask with the schema and pick strategy 4: 2 second tries, 1 form sent to a person, note 12, and 15 passed on, every value written in its note.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the register room is haunted. The schema demanded an age, a time and one of three causes, and structured outputs let the model write nothing else, so for a note that gave only where and when he was found, it wrote the likeliest values the form allowed.

steps.title: Code reads fields, not prose.
steps.text: The register is a program, and a program can't read a sentence: it reads named fields. That is the point of structured output: a reply in a fixed shape that code can read. JSON is the usual way to hand it over. RFC 8259, the IETF's specification for it, calls JSON a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format, and says it can represent four primitive types (strings, numbers, booleans, and null) and two structured types (objects and arrays). A JSON object is a set of names with their values, like {"age": 67}. To use a reply, code first parses it, and parsing fails on anything that isn't JSON. Ysbrand's first program asked for JSON in the prompt with one filled-in example, the few-shot prompting of the last case. Anthropic's structured outputs page lists what that still lets through, even with careful prompting: parsing errors from invalid JSON syntax, missing required fields, inconsistent data types, and schema violations requiring error handling and retries. On last night's sixteen, in the sim, the old program gets 4 replies that won't parse, two sentences and two pieces of broken JSON, and 7 more that parse with a box wrong.

steps.title: A JSON Schema is the form's rules.
steps.text: JSON Schema's own site describes it as a declarative language for defining structure and constraints for JSON data: you write the rules down, and a validator, a program that implements them, checks each document. Ysbrand's schema uses the common ones. type says what a value must be: a string of text, an integer, which is a whole number, or null. required lists the fields that must be there, and the site points out that by default, the properties defined by the properties keyword are not required. enum is used to restrict a value to a fixed set of values: his three causes. minimum and maximum set a range: age from 0 to 120. pattern sets a text's shape: times like 05:10. And null, JSON's value for nothing, is a value of its own: the site's reference says that in JSON, null isn't equivalent to something being absent. So not known needs a decision in the schema: a union type such as ["integer", "null"], which allows a whole number or null, or an enum value such as unknown. Without one, a required box has no honest answer. The current version of the specification is called 2020-12.

steps.title: Three ways to get structure, weakest to strongest.
steps.text: First, ask in the prompt, with an example. It is cheap and works with almost any model, and nothing guarantees it. Second, the provider's own feature. Anthropic's page says structured outputs guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding: Always valid: No more JSON.parse() errors, and Type safe: Guaranteed field types and required fields. Constrained decoding builds on case 6's sampling. Willard and Louf describe the common approach as working out which tokens are valid, according to the constraints and previously sampled tokens, and setting the probabilities of invalid tokens to zero. The model still chooses; it just can't choose anything the schema forbids. The guarantee has edges, and the page lists them: structured outputs guarantee schema compliance in most cases. A refusal, with stop_reason refusal, or a reply cut off at max_tokens may not match your schema, and the capitalization of enum values isn't guaranteed. Only a subset of JSON Schema is supported. Numerical constraints such as minimum and maximum, and string lengths, are not: sent as they are, they get a 400 error, so most SDK helpers remove them first, and, in the page's words, a helper that validates responses still enforces every constraint in your code. Ysbrand's helper sent age as a plain integer, and his program never checked the reply against 0 to 120: that is how Ernest Vellacott became 1958. Third, validate every reply in your own code anyway, against the whole schema. The same idea runs through tools: Anthropic's strict tool use constrains a model's token sampling to schema-valid outputs for a tool's inputs. Case 5 of this season is tool calling, where schemas describe the tools a model may ask your app to run.

steps.title: When a reply fails, ask again once with the error, then fall back.
steps.text: Parse and validate every reply, and decide in advance what happens when one fails: never crash on it, and never pass it on. The usual first move is a retry with the error: ask again, with the validator's message added, such as age: 1958 is above the maximum, 120. This is not the retry from the first case of this season, which resends a request the provider refused or couldn't serve, such as a 429; here the request worked and the content was wrong. Bound it, here to one second try: each try costs tokens and time, and a loop that asks until something passes can run for a long time, or end with whatever happened to pass. Then fall back: a safe default where one really exists, a review queue for a person, or an error returned to the caller. Mind what the error asks for. In the sim, strategy 3 on the prompt-only replies asks again 11 times and fixes 6. But four notes that honestly left a box out, the man at Sallow Road's among them, were told that box is required, and came back with values made up to fill it. The error asked for an answer the note didn't have.

steps.title: Valid is not true.
steps.text: Every one of last night's forms fitted the schema the provider enforced. Six were wrong: Ernest Vellacott's age, and five forms holding values their notes never gave. The schema demanded an age, a time and one of three causes, and constrained decoding let the model write nothing else, so for a note that gave only where and when he was found, it wrote the likeliest values it was allowed. OpenAI's structured outputs guide is plain about it: although all fields must be required (and the model will return a value for each parameter), it is possible to emulate an optional parameter by using a union type with null. It also warns about the extreme case: the model will always try to adhere to the provided schema, which can result in hallucinations if the input is completely unrelated to the schema. A note with three of its boxes empty is a small version of the same thing. So give the schema an honest way out: null for an age or a time nobody knows, unknown in the cause list. Then add semantic checks, tests of what a value means that a schema can't express: is it written in the note, does it match the case file. They catch what the honest box misses. Even with unknown allowed, Isadora Fitch's form says natural, because her note says she looked peaceful: a model can still infer what it was never told. Hers goes to a person.

diagram.aria: The register program after the fix. Top row: the note, typed as written and the only evidence, goes to the model, with structured outputs on and unknown allowed; the model's reply goes to the checks in code, the whole schema and then the note, with one retry and the error added. Bottom row: the schema, kept as one copy in code, with null and unknown legal, gives the model the form; a form that passes every check goes to the register, which holds checked forms only, true to their notes; a form that fails twice goes to a person, after the second try, who decides or marks it pending. A note at the bottom says nothing unchecked reaches the register.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. Each typed note goes to the model with a schema that makes not known a legal answer. Every reply then goes through checks in code: the whole schema first, the rules the provider skips included, then whether each value is written in the note. A form that passes reaches the register. A form that fails is asked for once more, with the error added, and if it fails again it goes to a person, never to the register.

fix.title: The fix: honest boxes, checks in code, one more try, then a person
fix.text: Make not known a legal answer: age and time of death may be null, and the cause list gains unknown. Keep structured outputs, so replies arrive in shape, but validate every reply in your own code against the whole schema, including the rules the provider doesn't enforce, such as the age range. Check stop_reason too, since a refusal or a cut-off reply may not match the schema. Then run semantic checks: here, every value must be written in its note. A form that fails either check is asked for once more, with the error added. If it fails again it goes to a person's review queue, never to the register. Keep one copy of the schema in code and build both the request and the validator from it, so the two can't drift apart. In the sim this setup asks again twice, sends one form to a person and passes fifteen on, every value written in its note; the night of the post passed on sixteen, six of them wrong.

limits: A semantic check is only as good as its rule. Is it written in the note catches a value the note never held, but not the wrong one of two values a note does hold: Ernest Vellacott's 1958 passes it, and only the age range catches it. It would also flag a value a note implies without spelling out. Some checks need other data, such as the case file or the pathologist's report, and some need a person.

Unknown is an answer a model can overuse as well as avoid. Count how often each box says unknown, and keep reading an audit sample of the forms that passed every check, since nobody else will. Allowing null has a cost too: Anthropic limits parameters with union types, such as a type that includes null, to 16 across a request's strict schemas, because they are especially expensive to compile, and the first request with a new schema waits while its grammar compiles.

A schema kept in two places tends to drift: if the request's schema and your validator are written separately, sooner or later one changes without the other. OpenAI's guide strongly recommends native SDK schema helpers, or a CI step that generates the JSON Schema from type definitions (or vice-versa). Keep one copy and build both from it, and remember that a person's review queue only helps if someone works it every day.

explain.seniorTake: A schema is a contract about shape, not truth. Let the provider enforce the shape where it can, and validate every reply in your own code anyway. Design the schema so that not known is a legal answer, because a required box with no honest option gets filled, usually with something plausible. Add checks of meaning where you can, bound your retries, and give whatever still fails to a person. Nothing unchecked goes downstream.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: what structured outputs promise
realWorld.text: Anthropic's structured outputs page says the feature constrains Claude's responses to follow a specific schema, ensuring valid, parseable output for downstream processing. It explains why: without structured outputs, Claude can generate malformed JSON responses or invalid tool inputs that break your applications, and even with careful prompting you may meet parsing errors from invalid JSON syntax, missing required fields, inconsistent data types, and schema violations requiring error handling and retries. Its promise: structured outputs guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding. Always valid: No more JSON.parse() errors. Type safe: Guaranteed field types and required fields. Reliable: No retries needed for schema violations. They work by compiling your JSON schemas into a grammar that constrains Claude's output.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: where the promise stops
realWorld.text: The same page: while structured outputs guarantee schema compliance in most cases, there are scenarios where the output may not match your schema. A refusal comes back with stop_reason refusal and a 200 status code, is billed, and the output may not match your schema because the refusal message takes precedence over schema constraints. A reply cut off at max_tokens may be incomplete and not match your schema; the advice is to retry with a higher max_tokens. Structured outputs don't guarantee the capitalization of string enum values, so the page says to compare enum values case-insensitively, and avoid enum values that differ only in capitalization. Numerical constraints, such as minimum and maximum, and string-length constraints are not supported. Most SDK helpers remove them, and Claude receives a simplified schema, but a helper that validates responses still enforces every constraint in your code.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a grammar has a cost
realWorld.text: Structured outputs use constrained sampling with compiled grammar artifacts. The first time you use a specific schema, there is additional latency while the grammar compiles, and compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use. Parameters with union types, such as a type of string or null, are limited to 16 across all strict schemas in one request: the page says these are especially expensive because they create exponential compilation cost.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: strict tool use
realWorld.text: For tools, setting strict: true on a tool definition guarantees Claude's tool inputs match your JSON Schema by constraining the model's token sampling to schema-valid outputs (a technique called grammar-constrained sampling). Without strict mode, the page says, Claude might return incompatible types ("2" instead of 2) or omit required fields; its example is a booking system that needs passengers as an integer and might otherwise get "two" or "2". Case 5 of this season covers tool calling.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: a value for every field
realWorld.text: OpenAI's guide says Structured Outputs is a feature that ensures the model will always generate responses that adhere to your supplied JSON Schema, so you don't need to worry about the model omitting a required key, or hallucinating an invalid enum value. It calls Structured Outputs the evolution of JSON mode: while both ensure valid JSON is produced, only Structured Outputs ensure schema adherence. To use it, all fields or function parameters must be specified as required, and, in its words: although all fields must be required (and the model will return a value for each parameter), it is possible to emulate an optional parameter by using a union type with null.

realWorld.title: OpenAI: when the input can't fill the form
realWorld.text: Under Tips and best practices: if your application is using user-generated input, make sure your prompt includes instructions on how to handle situations where the input cannot result in a valid response. The model will always try to adhere to the provided schema, which can result in hallucinations if the input is completely unrelated to the schema. You could include language in your prompt to specify that you want to return empty parameters, or a specific sentence, if the model detects that the input is incompatible with the task. The next tip begins: Structured Outputs can still contain mistakes. To keep a schema and the code that uses it from drifting apart, the guide strongly recommends native SDK schema helpers, or a CI step that generates the JSON Schema from type definitions (or vice-versa).

realWorld.title: JSON Schema: rules, and a validator
realWorld.text: The JSON Schema site describes JSON Schema as a declarative language for defining structure and constraints for JSON data. It adds that while JSON Schema provides the language, validating a JSON instance against a schema requires a JSON Schema validator, which checks if the JSON documents conform to the schema. The language describes the rules; something still has to run them, on every document.

realWorld.title: JSON Schema: null is a value
realWorld.text: The reference page for null says: when a schema specifies a type of null, it has only one acceptable value: null. It's important to remember that in JSON, null isn't equivalent to something being absent. A box that may hold null is still there in every form; null is how it says nobody knows.

realWorld.title: JSON, 2017
realWorld.text: RFC 8259, published by the IETF in December 2017, opens: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. JSON can represent four primitive types (strings, numbers, booleans, and null) and two structured types (objects and arrays), and an object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs.

realWorld.title: Guided generation, 2023
realWorld.text: Brandon Willard and Rémi Louf showed an efficient way to guide a model's text generation with regular expressions and grammars, guaranteeing the structure of the generated text while adding little overhead. They describe the common approach as repeated evaluations over the entire vocabulary in order to determine which tokens are valid, according to the constraints and previously sampled tokens, and setting the probabilities of invalid tokens to zero. Their method is provided in an open-source library, Outlines.

asked: How do you get reliable JSON out of an LLM?
What do you do when the output fails validation?
How would you design the schema for an extraction task?
interview.answer: I use three layers. First I ask clearly, with the format and an example in the prompt, but I treat that as a hint, not a guarantee. Second, where the provider offers it, I use structured outputs or strict tool use, which constrain decoding to the schema, so the reply parses and has the right fields and types in most cases. I read that provider's limits: refusals and replies cut off at max_tokens may not match, enum capitalization may differ, and some keywords, such as minimum and maximum on Anthropic's, aren't enforced. Third, I validate every reply in my own code against the whole schema, with one copy of the schema that also builds the request, and I check stop_reason. When a reply fails, I don't crash and I don't pass it on: I retry once or twice with the validation error in the prompt, then fall back to a safe default if one genuinely exists, a review queue for a person, or an error to the caller, and I log every failure so I can see the rate per field. A schema only checks shape. It can't tell whether a valid value is true, and it can make things worse: under structured outputs, a required field with no way to say unknown forces the model to fill it, often with something plausible. So in an extraction schema every field the source might not contain is nullable or has an explicit unknown value, and the prompt says to use it rather than guess. I keep enums short and distinct, and after validation I run semantic checks: the value appears in the source, totals add up, dates are in order, IDs exist in our systems. Finally, I have a person read an audit sample of records that passed every check, because those failures are the ones nothing else will find.

terms.def: A model's output in a fixed, machine-readable shape, such as JSON that matches a schema, so code can read its fields instead of prose.
A provider feature that makes every reply fit a JSON Schema sent with the request, using constrained decoding. Anthropic and OpenAI both use the name.
A description of the shape data must have: which fields, and what each may hold. Ysbrand's schema is the register's form.
A standard way to write a schema in JSON: a declarative language for the structure and constraints of JSON data. A validator checks documents against it. The current version is 2020-12.
In JSON, a set of named fields and their values inside curly brackets, such as {"age": 67}. RFC 8259 calls it an unordered collection of name/value pairs.
One named value in a JSON object, such as age.
Ysbrand's word for a field on the register's form.
In a schema, the kind of value a field may hold, such as string, integer or null.
In JSON, a piece of text in double quotes, such as "05:10".
A whole number, with no fraction, such as 67. JSON Schema's integer type.
A field that must be present in every document. In JSON Schema it is listed under required; fields are not required by default.
In OpenAI's docs, a field or input that may be left out. Its structured outputs make every field required and suggest a type that also allows null instead.
In providers' docs, an input a function or tool takes, such as a booking's passengers. Not case 1's parameter, a number inside a model that training tunes.
A value that is either true or false.
In JSON, an ordered list of values inside square brackets, such as ["integer", "null"].
Saying what the result must look like, rather than the steps to produce it. A schema is declarative: it states the rules, and a validator applies them.
Code that declares the shape of a kind of data: its named fields and the type of each. Some tools turn it into a JSON Schema.
JavaScript's built-in function that turns JSON text into data. It throws an error on text that isn't JSON.
Here, turn a description, such as a schema, into a form a program can use quickly, such as a grammar.
Growing by multiplying, so each step adds far more than the last.
Short for enumeration: a fixed list of the only values a field may hold, such as natural, accident or exposure.
JSON's value for nothing. In JSON, null is not the same as a missing field: the field is there, and holds no value.
A type that allows more than one kind of value, such as ["integer", "null"]: a whole number, or null.
The lowest and highest values a number may take, set in JSON Schema with minimum and maximum. Ysbrand's age range is 0 to 120.
In JSON Schema, a rule for a string's shape written as a regular expression, such as a time like 05:10.
A short code for a text pattern, such as two digits, a colon and two digits. Programs use it to test or find text.
Here, a set of rules for which sequences of tokens are allowed. Providers turn a JSON Schema into one to constrain a model's output.
Choosing each next token only among those that keep the output valid under a schema or grammar; every other token gets zero probability.
Another name for constrained decoding. Anthropic's strict tool use page calls it grammar-constrained sampling.
Anthropic's setting, strict: true on a tool, that constrains a model's tool inputs to that tool's JSON Schema.
A model asking your app to run a function for it, with inputs described by a schema. Case 5 of this season covers it.
An older OpenAI feature that makes the output valid JSON but doesn't make it match a schema.
A model declining a request, for example for safety. With structured outputs a refusal may not match the schema; Anthropic marks it with stop_reason refusal.
Code that checks a document against a schema and says which rules it breaks. Ysbrand's is a few lines of plain code.
Here, matching every rule of the schema. Valid says nothing about whether the values are true.
A check of what a value means rather than its shape, such as: is it written in the note, or does it exist in our systems?
Here, a value in a form where the source said nothing, such as the age 64 for a man whose note gave no age.
Asking the model again, with the validator's message added, after a reply that arrived but failed a check. Not the same as resending a request that failed, such as one refused with a 429.
This case's name for one retry with the error. Every strategy here allows at most one.
What a program does when a step fails for good: use a safe default, put the item in a review queue for a person, or return an error to the caller.
A value a program can use when it has no answer, chosen so it can't be mistaken for a real one. A default that looks real is an invented value.
A list of items waiting for a person to check them. Dr Marsk's queue holds forms that failed twice.
The program or person that asked for a result, and gets the error if it fails.
A program stopping because of an error it didn't handle.
The parts of a system that use a result after it is made. The register is downstream of Ysbrand's program.
Here, hand a reply to the register, downstream.
Pulling fields out of free text, such as a date from an email, into a fixed shape.
A chain of steps that data passes through, each taking the last step's output.
A program that stores records so other programs can search and change them.
A few records picked, often at random, for a person to check by hand, to find mistakes that passed every automatic check.
A function in a provider's SDK that does a common job, such as turning a type in your code into a JSON Schema and checking the reply against it.
Part of something larger. Structured outputs support a subset of JSON Schema.
Treating capital and small letters as the same, so Natural and natural match.
A shared way of writing data so different programs can exchange it, such as JSON.
Request for Comments: a numbered document from the IETF. Some are standards, such as RFC 8259 for JSON.
The Internet Engineering Task Force, which writes the standards much of the internet runs on.
A reply written for this case to stand in for a model's, and labelled as such. The sim uses them; they measure no model.
Software whose code anyone may read, use and change.
The open-source library in which Willard and Louf provide their method for guided generation.
The official record of deaths an office keeps, one entry per death. Here it is a form with six boxes that Ysbrand's program fills in.
The person who keeps an office's records overnight. Ysbrand types up the night's notes.
The coroner's second in charge, who can act for the coroner. Dr Marsk reads the register each morning.
A doctor who examines the dead to find the cause of death, and writes a report on it.
Here, a cause of death on the form: harm from being out in the cold for too long.
Not decided yet. A record marked pending is completed when more is known.
A home where older or ill people live, with staff to look after them.
A buyer's numbered record of an order, which a supplier's invoice should refer to.
Code that converts data from one system's shape to another's.
Writing a date as year, month and day in numbers, such as 2026-10-07.
GDPR Article 5(1)(d): personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, and inaccurate data erased or rectified without delay.
Section 23 of Singapore's PDPA: a reasonable effort to make sure personal data is accurate and complete when it is likely to be used for a decision about a person or disclosed.
One of the optional categories of the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria: whether a system's processing is complete, valid and accurate.

atWork: Find one place where model output goes straight into a database or another system: an extraction pipeline that reads emails, invoices or forms, a classifier that tags tickets, a job that fills in records. For every required field, ask what the model writes when the input doesn't say. Then look for the answer in your data: values that turn up more often than the inputs could explain, such as midnight times, the first of the month, round numbers, or one category far ahead of the rest. A common incident: an extraction job writes model output straight into a database, the schema requires a field, and for inputs without one the model fills it confidently with a value that looks right and belongs to nothing, until someone downstream acts on it. The fix is the same as Ysbrand's: nullable fields or an explicit unknown, validation of every reply in code, one retry with the error, a review queue for what still fails, and an audit sample of passing records read by a person each week. Standards-readiness note: if those records hold personal data under the GDPR, its accuracy principle, Article 5(1)(d), asks that every reasonable step be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate data without delay; Singapore's PDPA has an Accuracy Obligation in section 23; and if your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes processing integrity, those criteria cover whether processing is complete, valid and accurate. An invented field is the kind of finding an audit makes, and building nullable fields, validation, a review queue and audit sampling in from the first version costs far less than adding them before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your team uses a model to read supplier emails and write each order into the orders database, with the provider's structured outputs switched on. The schema requires a delivery_date as YYYY-MM-DD. This month the warehouse found dozens of orders carrying delivery dates no supplier ever gave, all of them believable. No error was ever raised. What happened, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The schema forced a value: a required date with no way to say not known got filled with a plausible one
Make not known legal: let the field be null, or add an explicit unknown, and say to use it
Check meaning in code before writing: the date must appear in the email it came from, or match the order system
Validate every reply, retry once with the error, send what still fails to a review queue, and audit a sample of what passed

recall.model: The schema made every order carry a delivery date, and structured outputs only let the model write text that fits the schema. When an email gave no date, the model still had to fill the box, so it wrote a plausible one. The reply was valid, so nothing failed. I'd make the field nullable, or allow an explicit unknown, and tell the model to use it rather than guess. Then I'd check every reply in our own code: validate it against the whole schema, and run semantic checks the schema can't express, such as the date appearing in the email it came from. A reply that fails gets one retry with the error; if it fails again it goes to a review queue for a person, never straight into the database. I'd also have someone read an audit sample of orders that passed every check each week, and go back over this month's orders for dates no email contains.

recall.prompt: Why did the register record a time of death and a cause for the man at Sallow Road?
options: The model mixed his note up with another and copied that form's values across
Every box was required and the cause list had no unknown, so it wrote likely values
The structured outputs feature failed that night and let an invalid form through
The patrol's note held a time and a cause that Ysbrand typed in by mistake
recall.why: Structured outputs constrain the reply to the schema, and the schema required an age, a time of death and one of natural, accident or exposure. The note gave none of them, so the model filled each box with a likely value: 64, 02:40, exposure. The form was valid, and the feature worked as its documentation says. The note gave only where and when he was found.

recall.prompt: A teammate says: we've switched on the provider's structured outputs, so we can delete our validation code. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: The guarantee has gaps: refusals and replies cut off at max_tokens may not match the schema, so still parse and check stop_reason
Not every rule is enforced: on Anthropic's, minimum, maximum and string lengths aren't, so your code must check them
Valid isn't true: a value can fit the schema and still be invented, so keep semantic checks, an honest unknown, and a person for what fails

recall.model: Keep it. Structured outputs make a reply fit the schema in most cases, not all: a refusal or a reply cut off at max_tokens may not match, so we still parse every reply and check stop_reason. The feature also supports only a subset of JSON Schema: on Anthropic's, numerical constraints such as minimum and maximum, and string lengths, aren't enforced, and the docs say a helper that validates responses still enforces them in your code. Most of all, a valid reply isn't a true one. If a required field has no way to say unknown, the model fills it with something plausible. So the code stays, and grows: an explicit unknown in the schema, semantic checks of what the values mean, one retry with the error, then a person.

recall.prompt: In the sim, strategy 3 asked the prompt-only replies again with the validator's error, and no unknown allowed. What happened to the man at Sallow Road's form?
options: Told his three boxes were required, it filled them with an age, a time and a cause
It came back as a sentence again, so it failed twice and was returned as an error
It left the three boxes empty again, because the error said they could stay empty
It copied the age, time and cause from the form just before his on the night
recall.why: The first reply honestly left out age, time_of_death and cause, and failed the validator: each is required. Asked again with that error, and with no way to say not known, the second reply filled them: 64, 02:40, exposure. Valid, and untrue. With the semantic check off it was passed on; with it on, it failed again and was stopped.

recall.prompt: Which rule in Ysbrand's schema does Anthropic's structured outputs feature not enforce, so his own code has to?
options: That every one of the six boxes is present
That age is a whole number, not text
That age is somewhere from 0 to 120
That cause is one of the listed values
recall.why: Anthropic's page lists numerical constraints such as minimum and maximum among the JSON Schema features structured outputs don't support. Most SDK helpers remove them, and a helper that validates responses enforces them in your code. Required fields, types and enum values are enforced, though the page notes enum capitalization isn't guaranteed. Ernest Vellacott's 1958 was an integer, as promised.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The program has run all winter with honest boxes, checks in code, one more try and Dr Marsk's queue, which gets a form or two most nights. Now the state is moving every county onto its new electronic register. Its form has forty causes and no unknown, every field is required, and it rejects any record that doesn't fit. The state's contractor has written an adapter to send our forms on. It turns unknown into natural, an empty time of death into 00:00 and an empty age into 0, so that every record is accepted. Dr Marsk says her queue will finally be empty.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What would you tell the contractor, and what should happen to a form the state's register can't hold honestly?

keyIdeas.idea: The adapter invents in code: 00:00 and 0 are valid and untrue, the same failure as the night at Sallow Road
Keep not known honest: ask the state for a pending or not-yet-known option, or hold the record back until the cause is known
Check each form against the state's schema in our own code before sending, and give what can't fit honestly to a person, not to a filler value
Keep measuring: count the forms that wait, and audit a sample of what was sent

coldCase.model: Tell the contractor that the adapter does in code what the model did on the night at Sallow Road: it fills a box nobody can fill honestly, with a value that passes. 00:00 and 0 are valid and untrue, and once they're in the state's register, nobody downstream can tell them from real answers. Dr Marsk's queue going empty is the warning, not the win. I'd ask the state for a pending or not-yet-known option, since its form will meet unknowns from every county. Until it has one, a form that can't be sent honestly waits on a pending list a person checks, and is sent when the cause is known, or amended later if the state allows it. We'd validate every form against the state's schema in our own code before sending, so a rejection never surprises us, and we'd count how many forms are waiting each week and audit a sample of what was sent.

sources.title: Anthropic, Structured outputs (Claude Platform docs), read 7 October 2026: structured outputs constrain Claude's responses to follow a specific schema, ensuring valid, parseable output for downstream processing; JSON outputs (output_config.format) and strict tool use (strict: true); without structured outputs, parsing errors from invalid JSON syntax, missing required fields, inconsistent data types, and schema violations requiring error handling and retries; guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding (Always valid, Type safe, Reliable); guarantee schema compliance in most cases; refusals (stop_reason refusal), token limit reached (stop_reason max_tokens), enum value casing; not supported: numerical constraints such as minimum, maximum and multipleOf, string constraints minLength and maxLength, with a 400 error for unsupported features; most SDK helpers remove unsupported constraints, and a helper that validates responses still enforces every constraint in your code; schemas compiled into a grammar; first request latency, grammars cached for 24 hours from last use; parameters with union types limited to 16 per request

Anthropic, Strict tool use (Claude Platform docs), read 7 October 2026: strict: true guarantees Claude's tool inputs match your JSON Schema by constraining the model's token sampling to schema-valid outputs (grammar-constrained sampling); without strict mode, incompatible types ("2" instead of 2) or omitted required fields; the passengers example

OpenAI, Structured model outputs (API docs), read 7 October 2026: ensures the model will always generate responses that adhere to your supplied JSON Schema; the evolution of JSON mode, and only Structured Outputs ensure schema adherence; all fields must be required, and an optional parameter can be emulated with a union type with null; handling user-generated input, which can result in hallucinations if the input is completely unrelated to the schema; return empty parameters, or a specific sentence; Structured Outputs can still contain mistakes; avoid JSON schema divergence with native SDK schema helpers or a CI step

JSON Schema, What is JSON Schema? (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: a declarative language for defining structure and constraints for JSON data; validating a JSON instance against a schema requires a JSON Schema validator
JSON Schema reference, object (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: by default, the properties defined by the properties keyword are not required; the required keyword
JSON Schema reference, enum (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: the enum keyword is used to restrict a value to a fixed set of values
JSON Schema reference, numeric types (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: ranges of numbers are specified using a combination of the minimum and maximum keywords
JSON Schema reference, null (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: a type of null has only one acceptable value, null; in JSON, null isn't equivalent to something being absent
JSON Schema, Specification (json-schema.org), read 7 October 2026: the current version is 2020-12

Bray (editor), RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format, IETF, December 2017: a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format; four primitive types and two structured types; an object is an unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs

Willard and Louf, Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models, arXiv 2307.09702, 2023: guiding generation with regular expressions and context-free grammars; guaranteeing the structure of the generated text with little overhead; the common approach determines which tokens are valid and sets the probabilities of invalid tokens to zero; implemented in the open source library Outlines

Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 5(1)(d): personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate are erased or rectified without delay (accuracy)

Personal Data Protection Commission Singapore, Advisory Guidelines on Key Concepts in the PDPA, Chapter 16, The Accuracy Obligation (section 23 of the PDPA): a reasonable effort to ensure that personal data collected is accurate and complete if it is likely to be used to make a decision that affects the individual or disclosed to another organisation
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including the processing integrity category
